questions.question: On a cold, clear winter morning an electrician is commissioning a rooftop PV array and measures the open-circuit voltage of a 20-module series string. The reading is noticeably higher than 20 times the open-circuit voltage printed on the module nameplate. How should the electrician determine whether this string is acceptable for the installed inverter?
options: Record 20 times the nameplate open-circuit voltage as the string voltage, because readings taken in cold weather run high and are not usable for comparison.
Repeat the reading at midday when the modules have warmed up and compare that lower voltage with the inverter's maximum input voltage rating.

Multiply the module open-circuit voltage by the number of modules in series, apply the module temperature coefficient for the lowest expected ambient temperature at the site, and compare that corrected value with the inverter's maximum input voltage.
Divide the measured string voltage by the number of modules and accept the string if each module's share stays below the module's maximum system voltage rating.
questions.explanation: PV open-circuit voltage rises as cell temperature falls, so the highest string voltage the inverter will ever see occurs at the coldest expected temperature, not at the nameplate test condition. The string is evaluated by taking the module open-circuit voltage, multiplying by the number of series modules, then correcting with the module's voltage temperature coefficient for the lowest expected ambient temperature, and comparing that worst-case value with the inverter's maximum input voltage. Using the uncorrected nameplate total or a warm midday reading understates the peak voltage the inverter must withstand, and dividing the string voltage by the module count compares against the wrong limit, since maximum system voltage applies to the full string, not to one module's share.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-13, Sub-task B-13.02
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply energy-flow monitoring knowledge while the electrician services and maintains renewable energy generating and storage systems.

questions.question: At a PV combiner box, four parallel strings all show similar string voltage, but the combined output current is well below the value expected for the measured irradiance. What should the electrician do next to find the cause?
options: Replace the most accessible combiner fuse, since matching string voltages confirm each string is delivering its share of current.
Investigate the inverter and its load side first, because a break in one paralleled string path cannot reduce the combined output current.

Clamp each string conductor in turn while irradiance stays steady, then compare the individual string currents with one another and with the expected per-string value to identify the low or dead string.
Add the nameplate current ratings of the four strings, record that sum as the combiner output current, and accept the array without taking field current readings.
questions.explanation: A string with an opened fuse, a loose termination, or a broken conductor can still show near-normal voltage at the combiner, so voltage alone does not prove current is flowing. Measuring each string's current with a clamp meter under steady irradiance and comparing the readings to each other and to the expected per-string value isolates which path is contributing little or nothing. Swapping an accessible fuse guesses at the fault, blaming the inverter ignores that the four string currents add to make the output, and adding nameplate values only predicts what should flow without confirming what actually does.
questions.tip: For paralleled PV strings, similar voltage does not prove that each string is contributing current.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-13, Sub-task B-13.01
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply pv string voltage knowledge while the electrician installs renewable energy generating and storage systems.

questions.question: A high-voltage feeder insulation report shows one acceptable-looking resistance value, but there are no previous results, temperature correction notes, or phase-to-phase comparisons. Why should the insulation condition be reviewed as a trend instead of accepted from that single number?
options: Insulation condition is judged more reliably by comparable results over time and by the test method, temperature correction, cable history, and phase comparisons.
One unloaded insulation reading is enough if it is above zero and the cable has not tripped a protective device.
A normal downstream load test proves the insulation is suitable, so insulation test records are only needed after a failure.
The best comparison is any nearby feeder, even if its length, loading, age, and operating conditions are different.
questions.explanation: The correct answer fits because high-voltage cable insulation condition is evaluated from comparable evidence, not from one isolated value. Test method, temperature effects, previous cable history, and similar phase results help show whether the insulation is stable or deteriorating. Accepting one unloaded reading is a tempting shortcut, but it can hide a developing defect that only becomes clear when the result is compared under consistent conditions.
questions.tip: Trend information is strongest when the test conditions and comparison points are consistent.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-14, Sub-task B-14.01
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply cable insulation condition knowledge while the electrician installs high-voltage equipment.

questions.question: The diagram shows a high-voltage power path running from the source through main protection and distribution equipment to the feeder protection that supplies the connected load. After completing cable work, the electrician performs a controlled functional test with the balanced three-phase load at the end of that path drawing its rated 60 kVA at 4160 V. Approximately what line current should be expected in the conductors at the feeder protective device serving that load?
questions.explanation: The feeder protection in the diagram carries the full line current of the single balanced three-phase load downstream of it, so the load rating sets the expected reading. For a balanced three-phase load, S = √3 × V × I, so I = 60 000 VA ÷ (1.732 × 4160 V) = 8.3 A. The other values come from substituting an incorrect multiplier for √3: using about 1.4 gives roughly 10.3 A, a larger multiplier gives about 6.3 A, and a smaller one gives about 12.3 A. Only 8.3 A satisfies √3 × 4160 V × I = 60 000 VA.
questions.tip: Convert kVA to VA before using the three-phase current formula.
questions.diagramAlt: Power path from source through main protection, distribution equipment, feeder protection and a connected load.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-14, Sub-task B-14.02
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply high-voltage load current knowledge while the electrician installs high-voltage cables.

questions.question: A shielded 13.8 kV cable has been isolated, tested dead and grounded. While inspecting a stress-cone termination, the electrician finds faint tracking marks on the insulation surface just past the shield cutback. What should be checked to determine why the tracking has developed at that point?
options: Measure insulation resistance from conductor to shield and return the cable to service if the reading is at least as high as the commissioning value
Wipe the tracked surface with solvent, re-coat it with silicone grease and reinstall the protective boot over the marks
Re-measure the shield cutback and insulation shaving dimensions, confirm the stress-relief element sits fully over the cutback, and check for contamination or sharp shield strands
Wrap additional layers of high-voltage tape over the tracked area, since added insulation thickness removes the stress concentration
questions.explanation: Tracking just past a shield cutback is a symptom of concentrated electrical stress at the point where the shield ends. The stress-relief element must bridge that cutback by the exact dimensions specified for the cable, and the surface must be clean and free of protruding shield strands, because contamination or a sharp edge raises the surface stress further. A DC insulation-resistance reading is taken at a fraction of operating stress and will usually pass even where the geometry is wrong, so it proves nothing about the cutback. Grease and extra tape only cover the marks; neither changes the field geometry that caused them, so the tracking will continue and eventually puncture the insulation.
questions.tip: At high-voltage terminations, small preparation or placement errors can create concentrated electrical stress.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-14, Sub-task B-14.03
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply shield continuity knowledge while the electrician services and maintains high-voltage systems.

questions.question: During commissioning of a newly installed shielded high-voltage feeder, an electrician measures several volts on a shield section that the design shows as bonded at both ends. What should be done before the shield is accepted as installed correctly?
options: Treat the reading as the normal capacitive coupling found on any shielded cable and record the shield section as satisfactory
Re-terminate the shield to the nearest ground point on the cable tray and accept the section once the measured voltage drops
Order replacement bonding jumpers and connectors for the entire cable run before locating which shield connection is open
Carry out a point-to-point continuity check along the shield path and confirm each bonding connection is made at the location the design calls for
questions.explanation: A shield deliberately bonded at both ends is a closed path, so induced voltage should not appear on it. Measurable voltage indicates an open, loose or misplaced bonding connection somewhere in that path, and a point-to-point continuity check is what locates it. Capacitive coupling voltage is expected only where a shield is intentionally floating at one end, so accepting the reading as normal hides a real break. Bonding to the nearest tray steel may lower the reading while creating an unintended parallel path and circulating current. Ordering new jumpers for the whole run replaces hardware without ever identifying which connection failed.
questions.tip: A shield continuity concern should be resolved from the bonding design and field measurements, not from repeated energizing attempts.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-14, Sub-task B-14.01
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply phasing confirmation knowledge while the electrician installs high-voltage equipment.

questions.question: An isolated high-voltage cable is routed beside energized equipment, and the work plan calls for temporary protective grounding before workers contact the conductors. What hazard is this grounding step intended to control?
options: It controls hazardous voltage that could appear from stored charge, induction, or backfeed after isolation has been completed and absence of voltage has been verified.
It replaces the need to prove absence of voltage when the disconnecting device is visibly open.
It confirms the cable insulation is serviceable by allowing normal load current to flow through the grounding set.
It is used only to identify phase rotation and has no role in worker protection after isolation.
questions.explanation: Temporary protective grounding is applied using the approved sequence, rated equipment, and identified connection points after isolation and absence-of-voltage verification. It helps control voltage that may appear from stored energy, induction from nearby energized circuits, or backfeed. The tempting shortcut is to treat an open isolating device as sufficient, but isolation alone does not prove the conductor will remain at a safe potential for contact.
questions.tip: Isolation, verification, discharge, and approved grounding are separate safety steps; one does not replace the others.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-14, Sub-task B-14.02
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply equipment clearances knowledge while the electrician installs high-voltage cables.

questions.question: A maintenance crew is checking the loading record for a high-voltage feeder before returning serviced equipment to operation. The connected balanced three-phase load is 120 kVA at 4160 V. Approximately what line current does that load draw?
questions.explanation: The correct result uses the three-phase apparent power relationship S = √3 × V × I. With 120 kVA at 4160 V, the expected line current is about 16.7 A. The other values are plausible if the three-phase factor is omitted, the apparent power is handled incorrectly, or the calculation is rounded from the wrong intermediate value.
questions.tip: For balanced three-phase kVA problems, use line voltage with the √3 factor.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-14, Sub-task B-14.03
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply high-voltage load current knowledge while the electrician services and maintains high-voltage systems.

questions.question: While commissioning metal-clad high-voltage switchgear, an electrician notices the load-break switch operating handle can begin to move even though the grounding switch position indicator reads closed. What must be completed before this cubicle is accepted?
options: Adjust the grounding switch position indicator until it agrees with the observed handle travel, then note the indication as corrected
Accept the interlock as functional, since the switch cannot be closed electrically while the grounding switch indicator reads closed

With the gear de-energized and grounded, cycle the mechanism through its full sequence to confirm handle travel is blocked with the grounding switch closed and that indication matches actual blade position
Block the handle in position and tag the cubicle so operators leave it alone until the next scheduled shutdown
questions.explanation: A mechanical interlock is only proven by operating it. With the equipment safe, running the mechanism through its complete sequence shows whether handle travel is actually blocked while the grounding switch is closed, and confirms the indicator agrees with the real blade position. Re-adjusting the indicator assumes the indication is wrong when it may be truthful, and it masks a mechanism that no longer blocks travel. Relying on an electrical close block ignores the fact that a manual handle can still be operated. Blocking and tagging the handle defers the problem and leaves an unverified interlock in an energized lineup, where a switching error could close onto a grounded bus.
questions.tip: Interlock acceptance depends on the approved sequence and verified positions, not just on whether the equipment can be energized.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-14, Sub-task B-14.01
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply interlock operation knowledge while the electrician installs high-voltage equipment.

questions.question: Refer to the power-path diagram. A high-voltage cable crew has been given an approved switching package for work on the load shown at the end of the path. The package requires isolation at the feeder protection device located between the distribution equipment and that connected load, and the switching sheet contains read-back and final-status boxes. Several feeder cubicles in the lineup carry similar field tags. What comparison is required for that feeder protection device before the documentation is accepted for field use?
options: Accept the package once a voltage indication taken on the load side of the feeder protection device reads normal, then fill in the switching sheet after the cable work is finished.

Compare the approved switching sequence, the identifier of the feeder protection device shown between the distribution equipment and the load, the read-back records, and the intended final status against the approved drawings and required switching outcome, and stop for clarification if they do not agree.
Use the recorded final status of the main protection device at the source end of the path as the reference, since the feeder protection device is supplied through the same distribution equipment.
Confirm only that the feeder cubicle can be operated from its handle, and take the device identifier from the field tag on the cubicle instead of from the approved drawings.
questions.explanation: The switching package must be checked against the approved drawings so the sequence, the exact identifier of the feeder protection device between the distribution equipment and the load, the read-back entries, and the required final status all agree; any disagreement is resolved before work is accepted. Similar field tags in a lineup make positive identification of that one device critical. A single normal voltage indication, the status of the upstream main protection, or a field tag read on its own does not prove that the correct device was selected and left in the required state.
questions.diagramAlt: Power path from source through main protection, distribution equipment, feeder protection and a connected load.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-14, Sub-task B-14.02
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply test-result trend knowledge while the electrician installs high-voltage cables.

questions.question: A maintenance record for a high-voltage feeder shows insulation-resistance results taken over several shutdowns. The latest value is not below the site acceptance limit, but one phase has steadily decreased while the other phases have remained consistent. Which statement best connects that trend information to a safe return-to-service decision?
options: High-voltage cable insulation results should be reviewed as comparable trends, using consistent test method information, temperature adjustment where applicable, cable history, and phase-to-phase comparison.
A single acceptable reading is enough to return the feeder to service because a pass at the latest inspection cancels earlier results.
The feeder should be judged by the downstream load nameplate first; insulation history can be reviewed later if the fault becomes permanent.
The most accessible termination should be replaced immediately because any declining phase trend proves that component is defective.
questions.explanation: The correct statement fits because insulation condition is better evaluated by comparing like test conditions, corrected or documented conditions, previous results, and differences between phases. A declining phase can be an early warning even when the latest value is still usable. The tempting single-reading approach fails because it can miss developing deterioration that is only visible as a trend.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-14, Sub-task B-14.03
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply access control knowledge while the electrician services and maintains high-voltage systems.

questions.question: A commissioning sheet for a 4.16 kV three-phase feeder lists a balanced temporary test load of 75 kVA. The measured values are steady, and the electrician wants to confirm the expected line current before comparing it with the approved test record. Approximately what line current should be expected?
questions.explanation: For a balanced three-phase load, apparent power is related to line voltage and line current by S = √3 × V × I. The 10.4 A result fits the supplied 75 kVA and 4160 V values. Choosing a nearby value without using the three-phase factor would give a misleading comparison to the expected commissioning current.
questions.tip: Convert kVA to VA and use the line-to-line voltage in the three-phase apparent-power formula.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-14, Sub-task B-14.01
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply high-voltage load current knowledge while the electrician installs high-voltage equipment.

questions.question: An extra-low-voltage control transformer for a door-hold circuit is checked before connection. With no load connected, the secondary voltage is lower than expected, and the apprentice suggests that the winding is damaged. What should be verified before accepting that conclusion?
options: Record the low secondary voltage as failed winding insulation and close the inspection without further checks.
Copy the connection arrangement from a similar transformer on another floor because it feeds the same type of device.
Compare the nameplate ratio, tap or selectable input position, measured primary voltage, and no-load secondary voltage with the approved design and manufacturer information.
Energize the connected load; if the load operates, assume the transformer ratio is correct.
questions.explanation: The correct action fits because an unexpected secondary voltage can result from the applied primary voltage, the selected input or tap, or the actual transformer ratio. Comparing those items with the approved design and manufacturer information identifies whether the result is acceptable. The tempting assumption of winding damage fails because it treats a symptom as a cause and can lead to replacing or reconnecting the wrong equipment.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-15, Sub-task B-15.01
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply turns ratio knowledge while the electrician installs extra-low-voltage transformers.

questions.question: Two single-phase transformer secondary windings are to be interconnected to supply a control circuit, following an approved connection diagram. The terminals carry markings, but the crew must confirm the winding relationship before the final connection is accepted. What comparison best verifies winding polarity?
options: Compare the nameplate polarity data, the terminal markings, the approved connection diagram, and the result of a suitable polarity test before making or accepting the final connection.
Energize one winding at reduced voltage and accept the polarity if the measured no-load voltage of that winding matches its nameplate value.
Copy the lead arrangement used on an identically rated transformer in the same enclosure, since equal ratings mean the terminals are marked in the same order.
Check the leads with an ohmmeter and connect the pair of leads that shows the lowest resistance reading between the two windings.
questions.explanation: Winding polarity describes the instantaneous relationship between identified terminals, so it is confirmed by reading the nameplate polarity information and terminal markings, following the approved connection diagram, and proving the relationship with a polarity test. A correct no-load voltage on one winding only shows that winding's ratio; it says nothing about how two windings will add or oppose once joined. Ratings shared with another transformer do not guarantee identical lead marking, and a resistance reading identifies continuity within a winding rather than which ends are of the same instantaneous polarity.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-15, Sub-task B-15.02
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply primary-secondary voltage knowledge while the electrician installs low-voltage single-phase transformers.

questions.question: A three-phase transformer is being commissioned for a mixed load that requires specific line-to-line voltage and an available neutral. Which statement best describes why the selected three-phase winding connection must be confirmed?
options: The winding connection affects phase displacement, line-to-line voltage, whether a line-to-neutral supply is available, phase sequence checks, and the intended grounding arrangement.
If the transformer energizes without immediate noise or trip, the three-phase connection has been proven acceptable.
A connection used successfully on another project should be repeated unless the load fails after energization.
Correct line-to-line voltage alone proves the neutral point is available and correctly connected.
questions.explanation: The correct statement fits because the three-phase connection determines more than whether voltage appears at the terminals; it affects phase relationship, available voltage system, neutral availability, and grounding method. The tempting line-to-line-voltage-only approach fails because a transformer can show acceptable line voltage while still lacking the expected neutral or having an unsuitable connection for the load.

questions.question: Refer to the transformer concept diagram. The primary winding shown has 500 turns and is supplied at 600 V. The secondary winding shown must deliver 240 V to a shop lighting panel. Assuming an ideal transformer, approximately how many turns are needed on that secondary winding?
options: 175 turns
200 turns
225 turns
250 turns
questions.explanation: In an ideal transformer the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio, so the secondary turns are found from Ns = Np x (Vs / Vp) = 500 x (240 / 600) = 500 x 0.4 = 200 turns. Checking the other values against the same ratio shows why they do not fit: 250 turns would give 300 V, 225 turns about 270 V, and 175 turns about 210 V, none of which match the required 240 V.

steps.label: Set up the ratio
steps.content: Vp ÷ Vs = Np ÷ Ns, so Ns = Np × Vs ÷ Vp.

questions.tip: Keep primary voltage with primary turns and secondary voltage with secondary turns when setting up the ratio.

questions.question: A facility reports low secondary voltage on a transformer early in the morning, and a proposed response is to move the tap upward immediately. Before the tap position record is accepted or changed, what evidence should be compared?
options: Replace the tap-changing component and adjust the related setting at the same time so the voltage complaint is cleared quickly.
Clear the recorded indication, re-energize repeatedly, and investigate only if protection operates again.
Compare measured primary voltage, measured secondary voltage, loading at the time of measurement, present tap position, and the approved tap chart with the design requirement.
Raise the tap until the secondary voltage appears acceptable, then record the new position without checking supply conditions.
questions.explanation: The correct comparison fits because secondary voltage is affected by supply voltage, loading, and the selected tap. Checking the present tap against the approved tap chart and measured conditions shows whether a tap change is justified. The tempting immediate adjustment fails because it may overcorrect the transformer if the low primary voltage or load condition later returns to normal.

questions.question: A 75 VA extra-low-voltage dry-type transformer is to be mounted above a suspended ceiling in a security panel room. The layout now shows cable trays and stored maintenance filters close to the proposed enclosure location. Which planning-review check gives the best basis for accepting the transformer cooling path?
options: Verify the proposed clearances, ventilation openings, expected room temperature, connected load, and any temperature trend against the approved layout and manufacturer instructions.
Accept the location if the transformer nameplate matches the design, because the nameplate rating already accounts for any nearby obstructions.
Plan to energize the transformer first and relocate it only if the secondary voltage drops under load.
Increase the overcurrent protection to reduce nuisance operation if the enclosure becomes warmer after ceiling tiles are installed.
questions.explanation: The correct check uses the evidence that directly affects heat removal: physical clearances, ventilation openings, ambient temperature, load, and observed temperature behaviour, compared with the approved design and manufacturer requirements. Relying on the nameplate alone is tempting, but it does not prove that the installed location can dissipate heat. Changing protection would not correct restricted cooling and could reduce fault protection.

questions.question: A small single-phase control transformer trips its upstream protective device only at the instant it is energized, then tests normal when isolated. What should the apprentice understand about inrush before the protection is coordinated?
options: Repeatedly reset the device until the core becomes magnetized enough to stop tripping.
Short-duration magnetizing current can occur at energization, so the protective device must be selected and set to ride through inrush while still clearing real faults.
Raise the protective setting until all energizing trips disappear, then record the setting as acceptable without further review.
Replace the transformer whenever energizing current is higher than normal full-load current.
questions.explanation: Transformer energization can produce a brief magnetizing inrush that is much higher than running current, so coordination must compare transformer data, energization characteristics, protective-device performance, and any event record. Repeated resetting is a tempting shortcut, but it does not distinguish normal inrush from a fault and may stress equipment. Simply raising settings can leave the circuit under-protected.

questions.question: A shop-built three-phase control assembly uses an ideal transformer winding set with 500 primary turns connected to a 600 V supply. The required secondary voltage for the control circuit is 120 V. Approximately how many secondary turns are needed on each matching secondary winding?
options: 75 turns
100 turns
125 turns
150 turns
questions.explanation: For an ideal transformer, the voltage ratio follows the turns ratio. A 120 V secondary from a 600 V primary is one-fifth of the primary voltage, so the secondary needs one-fifth of the primary turns. Choosing 125 turns would apply the wrong ratio and would produce a secondary voltage higher than intended.

steps.label: Set up the ratio
steps.content: Vp ÷ Vs = Np ÷ Ns, so Ns = Np × Vs ÷ Vp.

questions.tip: Keep the primary voltage with the primary turns and the secondary voltage with the secondary turns.

questions.question: The dry-type transformer feeding a new lighting distribution section is connected as shown in the concept diagram, where the winding on the secondary side has fewer turns than the primary winding. The owner reports that the transformer runs hottest late in the afternoon, when only some of the panels supplied from that secondary winding appear heavily loaded. Before accepting the secondary loading, what comparison should be made?
options: Record one no-load secondary voltage reading at a panel and accept the installation if it matches the value predicted by the turns relationship shown in the diagram.
Compare the measured phase currents, secondary voltage, afternoon load profile, and winding temperature rise against the transformer kVA rating and the approved design load calculation.
Compare the turns relationship shown in the diagram with the voltage ratio stamped on the nameplate and accept the loading once the two ratios are found to agree.
Measure only the primary current during the afternoon peak and accept the loading if it stays below the rating of the primary overcurrent device.
questions.explanation: The turns relationship in the diagram sets the secondary voltage, but it says nothing about how much current the secondary winding is actually carrying. Accepting secondary loading requires comparing measured per-phase secondary current, voltage, how long the peak lasts, and temperature rise against the kVA rating and the design load calculation, because heating follows current and load duration. A single no-load voltage reading or a ratio check confirms the transformer relationship but hides overload and phase imbalance, and primary current alone can look acceptable while one heavily loaded secondary phase overheats.

questions.question: A 45 kVA dry-type transformer in a plant switchroom kept running for several hours after its cooling fan seized. When the electrician locks it out and opens the enclosure, there is a faint scorched odour and light brown discolouration on the coil surfaces near the ventilation openings. Which evidence should decide whether the winding insulation is still fit for the transformer to be returned to service?
options: Close visual examination of the coil surfaces and varnish for cracking, blistering, or carbon tracking once the windings have fully cooled.
Insulation resistance readings taken at the manufacturer's recommended test voltage, corrected for winding temperature and compared with the unit's earlier test records.
Secondary voltage and phase currents measured under load, confirming that the ratio and the current balance stay within the transformer's normal ranges.
Winding resistance measured phase by phase with a low-resistance ohmmeter, with the three readings agreeing within a few percent of one another.
questions.explanation: Losing cooling airflow lets the winding temperature climb past the insulation system's rated limit, and that heat ages the insulating material rather than the copper. Insulation condition is judged by insulation resistance testing at the voltage the manufacturer specifies, with the result corrected to a common temperature so it can be compared fairly against earlier readings for that unit; a marked drop from the previous trend points to heat-degraded insulation even when the transformer would still operate. A visual check of the coils may reveal discolouration or tracking and is worth doing, but sound-looking varnish can still cover insulation whose dielectric strength has been reduced, so appearance alone cannot clear the unit. Secondary voltage and phase currents reflect turns ratio and connected load, not the dielectric strength between turns or to ground. Winding resistance readings verify conductor continuity and connection quality, so they would catch a broken or high-resistance joint but tell nothing about the insulation surrounding the conductors.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-15, Sub-task B-15.05

questions.question: A door operator uses an extra-low-voltage transformer with selectable primary taps. Before the electrician connects the secondary control circuit, why is transformer ratio included in the inspection?
options: The ratio check confirms that the winding relationship, selected tap, measured primary voltage, and no-load secondary voltage will produce the intended control voltage.
The ratio check is mainly used to prove that the transformer enclosure is bonded.
Transformer ratio only matters after the load is connected and the operator has completed several cycles.
If the secondary voltage is off target, the usual correction is to increase protective-device rating until the voltage stabilizes.
questions.explanation: Transformer ratio links primary voltage, selected tap, winding turns, and expected secondary voltage, so checking it before connection helps prevent applying the wrong voltage to extra-low-voltage equipment. Waiting until after cycling the load is tempting, but a wrong ratio can damage controls before the problem is noticed. Changing protection does not correct an incorrect tap or winding relationship.

questions.question: A replacement single-phase low-voltage transformer is being checked on the bench because the field tag is faded. The ideal transformer has 500 primary turns for a 600 V primary, and the required secondary is 208 V. Approximately how many secondary turns are required?
options: 148.3 turns
173.3 turns
198.3 turns
223.3 turns
questions.explanation: For an ideal transformer, voltage ratio equals turns ratio. The 208 V secondary is 208/600 of the primary voltage, so the secondary turns must be the same fraction of 500 primary turns. Selecting 198.3 turns would use an incorrect ratio and would not match the intended secondary voltage.
questions.tip: Use the same side of the transformer for each voltage-and-turns pair when setting up the ratio.

questions.question: A three-phase transformer bank is being reconnected after the terminals were cleaned and re-marked. Before the secondary conductors are landed on the load side, which field check gives the strongest basis for accepting winding polarity?
options: Take one unloaded line-to-line voltage reading on the secondary and accept the connections if the value is close to the expected secondary voltage.
Match the terminal arrangement to another transformer bank in the same room that supplies a comparable lighting and receptacle load.
Compare the nameplate polarity information, the re-marked terminal markings, and the approved connection diagram, then confirm the result with a suitable polarity test before landing the conductors.
Check continuity through each winding with an ohmmeter and accept the polarity if all three windings give similar resistance readings.
questions.explanation: Polarity describes the instantaneous relationship between primary and secondary terminals, so it must be established from the nameplate, the terminal markings as re-applied, the approved connection diagram, and a polarity test that actually compares the windings before the load-side conductors are landed. One unloaded line-to-line reading can look correct even when a winding is reversed within the bank, another bank's terminal layout may reflect a different internal connection or vector arrangement, and winding continuity or resistance readings confirm only that the coils and joints are sound, not which way each winding is oriented.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-15, Sub-task B-15.03

questions.question: A pad-mounted three-phase transformer is being checked before commissioning a building service. The measured secondary line-to-line voltages match the approved drawings, but the expected line-to-neutral voltage cannot be obtained at the distribution equipment. What should the electrician do before signing off the installation?
options: Accept the installation because correct line-to-line readings prove the three-phase transformer connection is suitable for all loads.

Keep the equipment from service and compare the approved connection/vector information, terminal links, neutral point arrangement, phase-to-neutral readings, and phase sequence against the required secondary system.
Install a temporary neutral from a nearby transformer so that the missing line-to-neutral voltage can be demonstrated during inspection.
Copy the terminal-link arrangement from a similar transformer on site, then energize and confirm that the connected equipment runs.
questions.explanation: The correct action is to hold the transformer out of service until the connection, terminal links, neutral point, measured phase voltages, and phase sequence match the approved design. Correct line-to-line voltage alone can still occur with a secondary connection that does not provide the required neutral. The tempting approach of accepting the job based only on line-to-line readings fails because single-phase line-to-neutral loads could be supplied from an unintended or unavailable voltage reference.
questions.tip: For three-phase transformer checks, prove both the voltage system and the phase relationship—not just one voltage reading.
questions.sourceReference: MWA B, Task B-15, Sub-task B-15.04

questions.question: The diagram shows a two-winding transformer with the primary voltage applied across the primary turns and the secondary voltage developed across the secondary turns. A maintenance electrician measures a dry-type transformer's secondary voltage as slightly low while the incoming primary supply is steady and the load is within its normal range. Which quantity shown in the diagram is actually altered when the electrician moves to a different tap, and how is that change carried out?
options: The number of winding turns actually in service, which changes the primary-to-secondary turns ratio shown, selected from the nameplate tap chart with the transformer isolated and verified de-energized.
The primary voltage applied to the winding shown on the input side, because moving to a different tap raises the supply value delivered by the utility to the transformer.
The phase relationship between the primary and secondary windings shown, so secondary rotation is corrected by moving the tap links to a different lettered position.
The impedance of the secondary winding shown, which sets available fault current, so the tap setting used on a similar nearby transformer can simply be copied.
questions.explanation: Tap connections bring more or fewer winding turns into the circuit, so the primary-to-secondary turns ratio in the diagram is what changes. With the primary voltage fixed, a smaller number of energized primary turns raises the secondary voltage, and a larger number lowers it, which is how a slightly low secondary reading is corrected. The tap must be chosen from the nameplate tap chart with the transformer isolated and verified de-energized, since tap links are live parts in normal operation. A tap change does not alter the incoming supply voltage, which is set by the utility and the feeder. It also does not change winding phase relationships or rotation, which depend on connection and lead identification, not tap position. Winding impedance and available fault current are design characteristics, and copying another unit's tap ignores differences in its supply voltage, loading, and nameplate values.
questions.tip: Before changing taps, record primary voltage, secondary voltage, load condition, and present tap position, then compare them with the approved tap chart.

questions.question: A control cabinet requires an extra-low-voltage transformer secondary of 24 V. The ideal transformer being selected has a 600 V primary winding with 1250 primary turns. Approximately how many secondary turns are required?
options: 25 turns
40 turns
50 turns
75 turns
questions.explanation: For an ideal transformer, the voltage ratio and turns ratio are proportional. A 24 V secondary from a 600 V primary requires the secondary turns to be the same fraction of the primary turns as 24 is of 600. Choosing 40 turns would understate the required turns ratio and would not produce the intended secondary voltage in the ideal calculation.

steps.label: Set up the ratio
steps.content: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns, so Ns = Np × Vs ÷ Vp.

questions.tip: Keep voltage and turns from the same winding on the same side of the ratio.

questions.question: A newly installed low-voltage single-phase transformer trips the upstream device immediately when energized with the secondary load disconnected. Insulation checks and visual inspection show no damage, and the event occurs only at the moment of switching. What should control the electrician’s next decision?
options: Repeatedly re-energize the transformer until the magnetic core happens to energize at a favourable point on the voltage wave.
Replace the upstream device with a larger one immediately, because instantaneous tripping at energization always proves the device is too small.

Treat the condition as possible transformer inrush, then verify isolation, confirm there is no secondary fault, and compare the transformer manufacturer’s inrush data, approved drawings, and protective-device characteristics before escalating or changing equipment.
Reconnect the secondary load so the load current will absorb the inrush current and prevent nuisance tripping.
questions.explanation: The evidence points to a possible inrush issue because the trip occurs only at energization and the secondary load is disconnected, but the electrician still must verify safe isolation and rule out faults before changing protection. Manufacturer data, approved drawings, and the protective device characteristics determine whether the installation is acceptable or needs escalation. The tempting response of simply installing a larger device fails because it can reduce protection without proving the cause or confirming that the change is approved.
questions.tip: Inrush is a switching event; do not solve it by trial-and-error energizing or unapproved protective-device changes.
